analysis.one_liner: Lets workers put 4% of their Social Security taxes into personal investment accounts while raising the retirement age to 68.
analysis.headline: Sen. Hagel's plan to let workers invest part of their Social Security taxes in personal accounts — paired with a higher retirement age and larger early-retirement penalties — drew zero cosponsors and never received a committee vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give workers born after 1960 (with the option to opt out) a personal "SAFE" investment account funded by 4% of their Social Security payroll taxes, managed centrally like the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan with an administrative fee capped at 0.57%. Workers could invest in stocks and bonds, the account would be their personal property, and any money left over after paying for their benefit would go to them in cash. To pay for this, the bill raises the full retirement age to 68, makes early retirement benefits much more costly to claim, scales guaranteed benefits down with rising life expectancy, and directs the Treasury to top off the Social Security trust funds from general tax revenue whenever they fall short.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers born after 1960 would own a real, inheritable investment account holding 4% of a lifetime of payroll taxes, invested in stocks and bonds with market returns, with a promise that their combined monthly benefit would be no lower than the benefit promised under today's Social Security. Wealth that today exists only as a government promise would become a legally owned nest egg. The investment industry would also gain: the fund would be run like the Thrift Savings Plan, which is administered by private contractors, and the bill orders a study of handing account payouts to private annuity sellers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Younger workers with new investment accounts

how_it_helps.text: Each worker born on or after January 1, 1961 would automatically get a SAFE account credited with 4% of wages and self-employment income each year, invested at the worker's direction among stock and bond funds (younger workers defaulted to 80% stocks), and could opt out entirely between ages 18 and 25.

The account would be the worker's sole property: at retirement, enough is converted to a guaranteed monthly annuity and survivor coverage, and any remaining balance is paid to the worker in cash at the worker's discretion; if the worker dies early, the remainder goes to the estate as a lump sum.
The SAFE Investment Fund would be maintained like the Thrift Savings Fund, and the bill promises a total monthly benefit no lower than the benefit promised under the current Social Security formula.

analysis.who_pays: Future retirees, through a higher retirement age (68 for those reaching early-retirement age after 2022), much steeper benefit reductions for retiring early, and automatic benefit reductions tied to rising life expectancy for anyone becoming eligible after 2023. Federal taxpayers also pay: the bill appropriates unlimited general-fund money to keep the Social Security trust funds fully funded while 4% of payroll income is diverted into the accounts, which means more federal borrowing.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the full retirement age to 68 for anyone reaching early-retirement age after 2022, and by 2028 makes the penalty for claiming early much larger (the benefit reduction per month of early claim rises from 5/9 of one percent to 25/36 of one percent), which cuts benefits most for workers with shorter life expectancies and physically demanding jobs.

For people first eligible after 2023, benefit factors are scaled down by measured increases in life expectancy, so guaranteed benefits fall automatically over time regardless of whether the trust funds are short.

Diverting 4% of payroll into personal accounts removes that money from the trust funds, and the bill answers this by appropriating whatever general revenue is needed to keep the funds' balances at 100% — an open-ended transfer financed by federal borrowing.

Account balances would rise and fall with the stock market, and each worker would pay an annual administrative fee of up to 0.57% of their account — modest by private-account standards, but a real annual charge on every dollar saved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is more worker-friendly than most 2005 privatization plans: it caps fees, runs the money through a low-cost government fund rather than Wall Street firms, and promises a benefit floor at today's promised level. But the same bill pays for that promise by cutting the guaranteed system itself — a later retirement age, much harsher early-retirement penalties, and automatic benefit reductions tied to longevity — and by borrowing whatever it takes to keep the trust funds whole during the transition. A worker who died young or was forced to retire early would bear the sharpest cuts, while the promised market upside depended on decades of returns and on Congress keeping the benefit-floor promise.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Hagel introduced the bill on March 7, 2005, during the nationwide fight over adding personal investment accounts to Social Security, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
Not a single other senator — Republican or Democrat — cosponsored the bill, despite Republicans holding the Senate majority at the time.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and its last entry in the congressional record is the March 7, 2005 referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers were better off because the bill died: none of its benefit cuts — the age-68 retirement age, the steeper early-retirement penalties, the automatic longevity reductions — ever took effect, and taxpayers were spared the open-ended general-fund spending the bill required. The financial industry gained nothing, since the personal-account system was never created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Retirees who kept today's benefit rules

for.name: Sen. Chuck Hagel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it, but recruited no cosponsors.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Spent early 2005 campaigning across the country for adding personal investment accounts to Social Security, creating the political moment for bills like this one.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to his committee and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it; the committee record ends with the March 7 referral.

against.name: AARP
against.what_they_did: Ran a major public campaign against carving private accounts out of Social Security in 2005, helping turn public opinion against the idea.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, but the partisan shape is clear from the record: the bill's only support was its Republican sponsor, and zero senators of either party — including the 55-member Republican majority — signed on as cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would route workers' accounts through a government-run fund modeled on the Thrift Savings Plan, which is administered by private contractors, and it orders a study on paying out accounts through annuities sold by private financial institutions. Gains would be real but limited, because the bill caps the administrative fee at 0.57% a year and keeps fund management centralized.

The bill requires the Treasury to transfer 4% of payroll income out of the trust funds into workers' accounts and then appropriate unlimited general revenue to keep the trust funds' balances at 100%, which means higher federal borrowing that ordinary taxpayers ultimately service. In exchange, the guaranteed benefit system gets a larger backstop than it has today.
